walkthroughs.body_html:
Databases — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Databases brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Databases.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The atomicity property of a transaction means:
options: The transaction either completes entirely or has no effect at all
Only one user may ever use the database
Each transaction must involve a single table
Transactions are stored in atoms of memory

mcqs.q: Uncontrolled data redundancy is a problem because it:
options: Wastes storage and risks inconsistent copies of the same fact
Makes the database completely unreadable
Is illegal in all countries
Prevents any data from being entered

mcqs.q: Is the DBMS the same thing as the database?
options: Yes - redundancy is required by data protection law.
No - the database is the organised collection of data; the DBMS is the software layer that manages access to it, like MySQL or Oracle.
Yes - DBMS is simply the technical name for the data itself.
Yes - deleting the DBMS deletes all the data automatically.

mcqs.q: Can you safely delete a customer record while orders still reference it?
options: No - referential integrity forbids leaving orphaned foreign keys; the DBMS will block the deletion or cascade it according to defined rules.
Yes - deleting the DBMS deletes all the data automatically.
Yes - the orders will automatically find a different customer.
Yes - deleting a parent record has no effect on other tables.

mcqs.q: Is data redundancy good because it acts as a backup?
options: Yes - the orders will automatically find a different customer.
Yes - redundancy is required by data protection law.
Yes - storing each fact several times protects against data loss.
No - uncontrolled duplication inside a database causes inconsistencies when copies diverge; backups are deliberate, separate, managed copies of the whole database.
